text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFormulate an isothermal sphere, locate the maximum mass at fixed external pressure, and distinguish a finite cloud from an infinite isothermal sphere. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A cloud has pressure at its boundary Consider a dense core inside a molecular cloud. Its surface need not have zero pressure: surrounding gas confines it. Truncate the cloud where its pressure equals an external pressure Pext. Assume a static, spherical, isothermal, nonrotating gas without magnetic or turbulent support. P = cs²ρ, dPdr = −GM(r)ρr², dMdr = 4πr²ρ Treat the sound speed as a spatially constant input. Heat exchange maintaining that temperature is a closure condition, not solved here. Raising external pressure can produce a denser core, but does not imply that any mass can remain in equilibrium. 02Construct the dimensionless isothermal sphere Write the density decrease as ρ = ρcexp(−ψ). Hydrostatic balance becomes cs²dψ/dr = GM/r². Choose a length a and dimensionless radius ξ, then express the problem as two first-order equations that can be integrated from the centre. a = cs√(4πGρc), r = aξ, M = 4πa³ρcm dψdξ = mξ², dmdξ = ξ²e−ψ 1ξ²ddξ(ξ²dψdξ) = e−ψ This differs from finite-index polytropes in both length scaling and boundary definition. Isothermal density does not vanish at a finite radius. Here the surface is where pressure matches the confining pressure. 03Start regularly at the centre Symmetry requires ψ(0) = ψ′(0) = m(0) = 0, but directly evaluating m/ξ² gives 0/0. Insert a series ψ = Aξ² + Bξ⁴ + … into the equation and compare coefficients to obtain regular starting values. ψ = ξ²6−ξ⁴120+ξ⁶1890+… m = ξ³3−ξ⁵30+ξ⁷315+… The panel starts with this series and integrates using fourth-order Runge–Kutta. Determine the dimensionless structure before matching physical density or mass. Halving the integration step also lets you check that the critical point is numerically resolved. 04Compare masses at fixed external pressure At an edge ξb, Pext = cs²ρcexp(−ψb). Eliminate central density to separate physical mass into a dimensional scale and a function μ. This μ denotes dimensionless mass, not mean molecular weight. M = cs⁴G3/2Pext1/2 μ(ξb), μ = m e−ψ/2√(4π) R = cs²√(GPext)ξb e−ψb/2√(4π) Varying ξb compares equilibria at fixed sound speed and external pressure, while central density and mass change. It is not a time animation of a single cloud moving along the curve. 05The mass maximum marks a stability boundary Differentiate μ and insert the two first-order equations. A turning point satisfies m² = 2ξ⁴exp(−ψ). The first maximum encountered along the regular central solution gives the following values. ξcrit ≈ 6.451, ρcρb ≈ 14.04 MBE ≈ 1.182 cs⁴G3/2Pext1/2 For this pressure-confined isothermal model, configurations before the first maximum are stable to small radial compression, whereas those beyond it are unstable. Identifying the turning point with radial stability uses a result of dynamical perturbation analysis; hydrostatic integration alone is not a proof about every possible disturbance. Magnetic fields, temperature gradients, rotation, and turbulence change the threshold. An observed contrast above 14 alone does not establish ongoing collapse. The Jeans chapter compares this finite cloud with an unbounded local model. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed sound speed, quadruple the external pressure. How do critical mass, critical radius, and the central-to-edge density contrast change? Show the answer and reasoning Critical mass and radius both scale as Pext−1/2, so both halve. The critical dimensionless radius is unchanged and the contrast stays near 14.0. Both absolute central and edge densities quadruple.
